title: HTML Lists
summary: Lists group related items and show whether their order matters.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: `<ul>` creates an unordered list, usually shown with bullets. The bullet says the entries belong together, but their order is not essential. It is like a basket of items to buy. Use it for navigation links, feature lists, and grouped choices when rearranging items would not change their meaning. In practice, a navigation menu is often an unordered list of links inside a nav region.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: `<ol>` creates an ordered list, usually shown with numbers. The sequence matters, such as steps to install a tool. It is like a numbered recipe. Browsers and assistive technology can communicate that sequence. Do not type numbers into ordinary paragraphs when the content is truly a sequence; a real ordered list can update its numbering automatically. In practice, numbered steps should remain numbered when their order matters to completing a task.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: `<li>` marks one item inside an ordered or unordered list. A list item can contain paragraphs, links, or another list. It is like one entry on a checklist. Keep each item focused so readers can scan it. Do not use `<li>` by itself; place it inside `<ul>` or `<ol>`. In practice, a nested list should be inside the list item that explains its relationship.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: A nested list expresses a smaller group that belongs to one parent item. For example, a travel plan can have a trip item with a short packing list inside it. It is like a folder containing a few related notes. Keep nesting shallow and meaningful, because deep lists are harder to scan and navigate. In practice, do not use list markup only to get default indentation in a visual layout.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Use a list when the items share a real relationship. Do not select list markup only because its default bullets create a visual indent. This is like choosing the right container for a group of objects. CSS can change bullets and spacing while the HTML keeps the group meaning for browsers and assistive technology. In practice, keep each item concise enough to scan while preserving the details people need.

foundations.overview: An HTML list groups related items so browsers and assistive technology can identify them as a group. Use an unordered list when order does not matter and an ordered list when sequence matters. Think of a shopping list versus numbered cooking steps. Each entry belongs in an `<li>` element. Choose lists because of the relationship between items, not simply to create indentation.
foundations.whyItMatters: Lists expose grouping and sequence to browsers and assistive technology. Correct structure helps people scan related items and understand which steps must happen in order.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser maps <ul>/<ol> to the ARIA 'list' role and each <li> to 'listitem', so screen readers announce 'list, 3 items' and let users navigate item-by-item. <ol> additionally renders and conveys numbering. Removing markers with CSS doesn't remove these roles; replacing lists with divs does.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Navigation menus (<ul> of links in a <nav>), recipe and tutorial steps (<ol>), feature/spec bullet lists (<ul>), product specifications and metadata (<dl>), and multi-level menus or category trees (nested lists).
foundations.businessImpact: Accessible, well-structured lists broaden reach to assistive-tech users (reducing legal risk) and give crawlers clean structure (helping SEO and rich results, e.g. how-to steps). Clear navigation also improves usability and conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Semantic lists are easier to style and maintain than ad-hoc div structures, work with built-in keyboard/AT behavior, and reduce the ARIA you'd otherwise need. Standard list patterns (nav as ul of li>a) are widely recognized across teams.
foundations.performanceImpact: Lists have negligible direct performance cost; the indirect benefit is leaner, semantic markup with fewer wrapper divs, which keeps the DOM smaller and CSS simpler than faking lists with generic containers.
commonUseCases: Navigation menus as a <ul> of <li><a> inside <nav>
Feature lists, tags, or ingredients with <ul>
Glossaries, FAQs, and key/value metadata with <dl>/<dt>/<dd>
Multi-level menus and category trees with nested lists

commonMisconceptions.myth: Use <ul> for bullets and <ol> for numbers — it's about appearance.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's about meaning: <ul> for unordered items, <ol> for sequences. Bullets and numbers are the default styling, which CSS can change or remove without changing the semantics.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can put text or divs directly inside <ul>/<ol>.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The only valid direct child is <li>. Content goes inside the <li>; nested lists go inside an <li>, not directly in the parent list.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Removing bullets with list-style:none makes it stop being a list.
commonMisconceptions.reality: CSS only changes appearance — the element still has list semantics and is announced as a list by assistive tech.

visualExplorer.title: Choosing the right list
visualExplorer.caption: A quick decision path from 'what does my content mean?' to the correct list element.

config.intro: There are three list types, and the right one depends on what your items mean — not on whether you want bullets or numbers.

steps.name: Is it term + definition?
steps.detail: If items are name/value or term/meaning pairs (glossary, specs, FAQ), use a description list: <dl> with <dt> and <dd>.

steps.name: Does order matter?
steps.detail: If the items form a sequence (steps, rankings), use <ol> so the numbering communicates order to everyone, including screen readers.

steps.name: Order doesn't matter
steps.detail: If items are just a set with no sequence (features, tags, nav links), use <ul>.

steps.name: Wrap items in <li>
steps.detail: Inside <ul>/<ol>, every item is an <li> — the only valid direct child. Nested lists go inside an <li>.

steps.name: Style with CSS
steps.detail: Change or remove bullets/numbers and lay items out horizontally in CSS; the list semantics stay intact.

interactiveExamples.title: Unordered vs ordered lists
interactiveExamples.explanation: The shopping list has no inherent order (<ul>); the recipe steps must happen in sequence (<ol>). The browser bullets one and numbers the other automatically.

files.index.html:
Shopping list

  • Apples
  • Bread
  • Milk

Recipe steps

  1. Preheat the oven to 180°C
  2. Mix the dry ingredients
  3. Bake for 30 minutes
files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 20px; }
h2 { margin-bottom: 4px; }

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A bulleted shopping list and a numbered, ordered recipe step list.

interactiveExamples.title: A description list
interactiveExamples.explanation: A <dl> pairs each <dt> term with its <dd> description — ideal for glossaries, specs, or metadata where each item is a name and a value.

files.index.html:
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The markup language that structures web content.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The language used to style web pages.</dd>
  <dt>JavaScript</dt>
  <dd>The language that adds interactivity.</dd>
</dl>

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Three bold terms, each followed by an indented description.

interactiveExamples.title: A nav menu and a nested list
interactiveExamples.explanation: Navigation is a <ul> of links inside <nav> with bullets removed via CSS — semantics kept, look changed. The second list shows nesting: sub-items live inside a parent <li>.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A horizontal navigation bar with no bullets, plus a nested category list with indented sub-items.

codeLab.title: Pick the right list type
codeLab.instructions: The 'Top 3 movies' content is a ranked sequence but uses a <ul>. Change it to an <ol> so the ranking is communicated. Keep the items the same.

files.index.html:
Top 3 movies

  • The First One
  • The Second One
  • The Third One

codeLab.expectedOutput: A numbered list (1, 2, 3) conveying the ranking.

files.index.html:
Top 3 movies

  1. The First One
  2. The Second One
  3. The Third One

hints: Ranking is a sequence, so the order matters — that means <ol>, not <ul>.
Just swap the wrapping element; the <li> items stay the same.

codeLab.title: Build a description list
codeLab.instructions: Convert these key/value spec lines into a proper description list: each label becomes a <dt> and each value a <dd>, wrapped in a <dl>.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A description list where each term (CPU, RAM, Storage) is followed by its value.
hints: The label (CPU, RAM, Storage) is the term → <dt>.
The value (8-core, 16 GB...) is the description → <dd>. Wrap all pairs in one <dl>.

keyTakeaways: `<ul>` creates an unordered list, usually shown with bullets.
`<ol>` creates an ordered list, usually shown with numbers.
`<li>` marks one item inside an ordered or unordered list.
A nested list expresses a smaller group that belongs to one parent item.
Use a list when the items share a real relationship.
